Does Store._reconcile violate the StoreIndex snapshot contract by writing delta rows into the live index.db in place?
Yes: _reconcile opens the live index read-write (self.connect()) and _reconcile_tables writes only-differing rows in place, so a read-only StoreIndex opened before a rebuild sees postings whose doc indices outrange the docs list it read at open (IndexError at similar.py:124).

evidence.note: Claim CONFIRMED on unfixed main: pytest tests/test_similar.py::test_a_store_index_outliving_a_rebuild_answers_consistently_from_its_snapshot -> IndexError at ddflow/services/similar.py:124 (1 failed in 0.73s). Mechanism traced: _reconcile opened self.connect() (live index.db read-write, WAL) and _reconcile_tables/_insert_similar wrote the tail rows in place, so the mode=ro StoreIndex opened before the rebuild read postings referencing doc indices beyond len(self._docs).

Edited ddflow/infra/store.py only (within task globs). _reconcile now backs up the existing index into a fresh temp file via the SQLite backup API, reconciles the tail rows into the copy, and publishes it through the new _publish swap shared with _build_into; the live index.db is never edited in place. Regression test test_a_store_index_outliving_a_rebuild_answers_consistently_from_its_snapshot: FAILED before (IndexError similar.py:124), PASSES after. tests/test_store.py 7 passed, tests/test_similar.py 45 passed.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_publish` is not atomic with respect to WAL sidecars: it unlinks `self.path-wal` and `self.path-shm` before executing `tmp.replace(self.path)`. If the live index is in WAL mode and has uncheckpointed commits, a reader that opens `self.path` after those sidecars have been removed but before the rename sees the old main database without its WAL; SQLite will then treat the WAL as empty and return only the last checkpointed state. That reader gets neither the old snapshot nor the new snapshot, contradicting the method’s stated contract and the `StoreIndex` snapshot-isolation requirement. The concrete interleaving is: reader opens `self.path`; `_publish` runs the sidecar unlinks and is preempted; the reader then reads and misses rows that were committed only in the now-deleted WAL.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_publish

chunk_findings.detail: The new `_reconcile` no longer takes any lock on the live index while it is copied and reconciled; the `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` was moved to the private temporary copy. Given two concurrent `Store.rebuild` calls (or a rebuild racing another writer to the same store), both can execute `src.backup(dst)` against the same pre-reconcile `index.db`. Process A reconciles its tail and `_publish` swaps it in; process B, still working from the stale copy taken before A published, then reconciles its own tail and `_publish` swaps that over, silently discarding A's committed rows. The original code’s live `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` would have serialized the writers and made the second reconcile see the first’s result. This lost-update window can leave the published index inconsistent with the event tail and can reintroduce snapshot/index mismatches.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/store.py:_reconcile

data.probe: The live index is never edited in place after this fix: _reconcile now writes only to a private -rebuilding temp file and self.path is solely replaced, so there are no uncheckpointed -wal/-shm frames on self.path at publish time; the unlink-then-rename sequence is byte-identical to the _build_into publish already on main, which the snapshot test pins. Ran pytest tests/test_similar.py: 45 passed, including test_a_store_index_outliving_a_rebuild_answers_consistently_from_its_snapshot (old reader answers from its snapshot) and test_rebuilding_twice_works_and_replaces_the_projection.

data.probe: Refuted: _reconcile is only ever called from _rebuild_locked (store.py:429), whose docstring states it is 'The ONLY write path. The caller holds lock_path', and _rebuild serializes every rebuild on _flock(self.lock_path, REBUILD_LOCK_TIMEOUT_S) before _rebuild_locked runs. Two concurrent Store.rebuild calls serialize on the flock: B blocks until A publishes and releases it, then re-checks stale() under the lock and reconciles against A's fresh index, so there is no stale-copy overwrite. The backup source is quiet under the flock (no writer commits mid-backup). Ran pytest tests/test_similar.py::test_concurrent_rebuilds_neither_traceback_nor_leave_a_broken_index: 1 passed (6 threads x 3 rebuilds, all 40 ids intact).
